sentences.text: The largest species, G. giganteus, stood about 2.15 meters tall and weighed up to 225 kilograms. Its skull was massive and powerfully built, featuring an extremely tall, compressed beak. This beak had a straight lip and lacked a raptorial hook. The animal possessed a relatively short neck made of at least 13 massive vertebrae.

The genus was named after Gaston Planté, who found the first fossils in the Argile Plastique formation near Paris. Edward Drinker Cope later discovered fragmentary remains in the Wasatch Formation, New Mexico, in 1874. The first nearly-complete skull and skeleton were found in the Willwood Formation, Wyoming, in 1916 and described in 1917. Hébert described the genus Gastornis in 1855.

There is a long-standing debate regarding the interpretation of Gastornis's diet. Gastornis species were historically considered predators of small mammals, including early equids. Evidence suggests Gastornis was likely herbivorous, feeding on tough plant material and seeds, rather than a predator. Researchers have suspected Gastornis was an ambush hunter or used pack hunting techniques to pursue prey through dense forests.

Gastornis is generally considered related to the Galloanserae, the clade containing modern waterfowl and gamebirds. Authors have placed both European and North American birds in the order Gastornithiformes or the family Gastornithidae. Gastornis and its relatives belong to the family Gastornithidae and were historically classified within the order Gruiformes. Upon recognizing the apparently close relationship between gastornithids and anseriforms, some researchers classified them within the anseriform group itself, while others restricted the term Anseriformes to the crown group of all modern species and named the larger group including extinct anseriform relatives, such as gastornithids, Anserimorphae.

Gastornis lived from the Paleocene to the mid-Eocene. It was an extinct genus of large, flightless birds living from the middle Paleocene to the middle Eocene. Most known fossils have been recovered from Europe, though species have also been reported from North America and Asia. Gastornis fossils found in western and central Europe date from the late Paleocene to the early Eocene.

It is debated whether Gastornis spread from Europe to North America via the Bering land bridge or via the Turgai Strait. The cause of Gastornis extinction is currently unclear. Competition with mammals is a debated factor in Gastornis extinction, despite coexisting with mammalian megafauna herbivores.
